items.title: Data + AI platform, end to end
items.prompt:
COMPLETE reference architecture — the canonical "end-to-end platform" shape.

This is JSONC (JSON + // comments) for YOU, the agent, to read and understand
(no comments) inside a ```json fence — strip these comments.

NESTED STRUCTURE, NOT PIXELS (reference/layout.md). The tab is a tree: each container
lays out its own children, and the renderer computes every position and size.
  • The top level is a row: the sources group, then the platform box.
  • The sources group is a column of four source tiles, `equal: "w"`.
  • The platform box is a row of two children: the platform stack (a column) and the
    Genie One tile (`track` `t1`). The wordmark and governance bar are children of that stack.
  • The platform stack is a column, top to bottom: the db-platform wordmark, the SQL
    lakehouse, a flow row, the Lakebase tile, then the governance bar.
  • The flow row is a row: the Lakeflow + Genie block, then a column of the three
    consumers (dashboard, apps, Genie Agent).
  • `track: "t1"` on the Lakeflow block, the Genie Agent and Genie One lines them up, so the
    path to the business user is one straight line.
  • Edges: `from`/`to` by node id. The `@handle` is inferred from geometry (left → right
    gives `@r` → `@l`). Name the ingest port on the target handle (see below).

LEFT → RIGHT story:
  sources → Lakeflow + Genie (one block) → lakehouse + lakebase
       → dashboard + Genie Agent + app → Genie One (business user built in)
  The db-platform wordmark sits at the top of the platform stack and the governance block
  at the bottom. One big white `box` wraps the Databricks components while external
  sources stay outside the platform boundary.

THE lakeflow-genie-block HAS THREE LEFT PORTS — the edge's target handle picks one:
  @in-lakeflow-connect  (databases / SaaS: Postgres, SAP…)
  @in-zerobus           (realtime / sensors / events — particle-stream flow)
  @in-direct            (files: PDF, CSV/Parquet dumps — travelling-docs flow)
  Right port `@r` → the compute layer. Inside the block = Genie Code + SDP
  (all bronze→silver→gold) — do NOT add separate sdp / genie-code nodes.

TABS: the top level is a JSON ARRAY — each element is one tab (its `name` is
the tab label). This file has one: the full end-to-end platform flow. (Emit
more tabs in the array when a diagram needs multiple views.)

items.prompt:
CUSTOMER ESTATE — how one customer's Databricks is laid out: identity, the
account, the workspaces per environment, the metastore and its catalogs, and
the customer storage behind them. Read reference/platform-model.md first.

architecture.md.

WHAT IT SHOWS (the facts that decide the shape):
  • The IdP is outside the account; users, groups and service principals are
    synced into the ACCOUNT (SCIM), then assigned to workspaces.
  • One metastore for the region. Workspaces and catalogs are SIBLINGS inside
    the account: each workspace is bound to its own catalog (edge), a catalog is
    never drawn inside a workspace.
  • The data sits in the customer's storage account, outside the Databricks
    boxes: managed storage per catalog, and an external location (path +
    storage credential) for files that land from elsewhere.
  • The NCC is account-level and attached to the workspaces; the network behind
    it is a separate tab (see the private connectivity references).

ADAPT IT: rename the cloud, region and environments to the customer's. Two
regions = two metastores (one per region), joined by Delta Sharing. Catalogs per
business unit go in the same column (`sales_prod`, `finance_prod`). Draw only
the environments, IdP and storage the request names.

DECISION VIEW — a comparison across environments, drawn as a shared grid.

JSONC (JSON + // comments) for YOU to read. Emit PLAIN JSON (strip //) in the
architecture.md ```json fence.

WHY THIS EXAMPLE. The other references teach a left→right FLOW. This one is the
COMPARISON/OWNERSHIP shape: platforms × environments in one plane, where the
point is "who owns what, and what crosses the boundary" — not how data moves
from A to B. Both axes carry meaning: the columns are platforms, the rows are
environments. Reach for it when the ask is a comparison. Do NOT impose this shape
on an ordinary flow: a flow is composed to its own structure.

WHAT THIS DEMONSTRATES:
  • Four columns in one row, one `group` per platform. Each column stacks its three
    environment tiles in the same order: dev, staging, production.
  • `track` names the environment: `t1` is dev, `t2` staging, `t3` production. Every
    column puts its dev tile on one line and its production tile on another, so the
    reader scans across and down.
  • The plane's title is the ownership statement: who runs the control loop, who
    executes, and which system is the record. A diagram that only places products next
    to each other leaves the reader to guess the operating model; say it.
  • The gateway and apps tiles sit in the last column: the gateway on the dev track, the
    apps tile on the production track.
  • ONE tight `desc` per tile. Nothing is a sentence. That is the text budget.
  • Every cross-boundary edge is LABELLED, and only those — the vertical promotion
    arrows are left bare because sequence is already obvious from position. Restraint is
    a device, not an omission.
  • The `story` names what the diagram does NOT show. See Step 1.6: a decision
    view legitimately compresses, but silent omission is indistinguishable from
    oversight.

WHERE IT DIVERGES from the other references: this is NOT a left→right data flow. It
is a comparison across environments, so the axis carries meaning in both directions:
columns are platforms, rows are environments. Reach for it when the ask is "who owns
what, and what moves between them", not "how does data get from A to B".

items.title: Genie Agent + documents
items.prompt:
GENIE AGENT + DOCUMENTS — one Genie Agent answers questions over governed
tables AND over PDFs held in a dedicated UC volume. This replaces the old
Knowledge Assistant + Supervisor Agent pair (both deprecated).

JSONC (JSON + // comments) for YOU to read. Emit PLAIN JSON (strip //) in the
architecture.md ```json fence.

WHAT IT SHOWS:
  • Two sources, two routes into ONE agent:
      – tables: Postgres → medallion → Genie Agent (`@out-gold`, SQL answers)
      – documents: PDFs → a dedicated MANAGED UC volume → Genie Agent
        (edge label "content search": the agent searches the files and cites them)
  • The volume is the document feed; it is NOT routed through the medallion.
  • Genie One is the business-user front door; the app calls the same agent.

STRUCTURE (reference/layout.md). The top level is a row: sources | platform box | Genie One.
  • The sources group is a column. `track: "tables"` and `track: "docs"` line each source
    up with the stage it feeds: Postgres with the medallion, the PDFs with the volume.
  • The platform box is a column: a banner row (the db-platform wordmark and the governance
    block, spread by `justify: "between"`), then a body row.
  • The body row is three columns: the data column (medallion over the UC volume), the
    answer column (Genie Agent over the Databricks Apps tile), and Genie One.
  • The two sources stay outside the platform box.

AUTHOR STRUCTURE, NOT PIXELS. See the medallion catalog row for `@out-gold`.

items.title: Genie One → custom MCP server on-premises
items.prompt:
GENIE ONE → A CUSTOM MCP SERVER ON-PREMISES, THROUGH A PRIVATE NETWORK GATEWAY (AZURE)

architecture.md. Read reference/style-networking.md first; the network part is the
same as reference/serverless-png-azure.jsonc (read its header for how PNG works).

HOW IT WORKS ON DATABRICKS (use this to adapt the diagram to the user's setup):
  • Genie One and the other Databricks AI services run on serverless, outside the
    customer's network. A custom MCP server that lives on-premises (or in a private
    VNet) is not reachable from there by default.
  • PNG supports serverless Azure Databricks Runtime products and AI services,
    including Genie One. So the network path is the ordinary PNG path: a managed NIC
    in a /28 subnet of the hub VNet (delegated to Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces),
    then the hub's VPN / ExpressRoute gateway to on-premises.
  • The MCP server is registered in Unity Gateway, which also holds its
    authentication. Genie One is then customized to use that registered server, so
    every call goes Genie One → Unity Gateway → (PNG) → MCP server.
  • Setup, in order: set up the PNG (Premium tier, /28 delegated subnet, NCC with the
    PNG attached to the workspaces); register the custom MCP server in Unity Gateway
    and configure its authentication; customize Genie One to connect to it.
  • PNG on Azure is in Public Preview; it is provisioned through the API only.

WHAT IT DEMONSTRATES (layout):
  • The same skeleton as serverless-png-azure, with the Databricks box split into the AI
    hops: Genie One → Unity Gateway → PNG (inside its NCC). The hops carry `track: "t1"`,
    so the red path is one straight line from left to right.
  • The workspace VNet is one card under the hub, joined by a dashed peering line:
    it exists, but the MCP traffic does not use it.
  • The on-prem side is ONE logo (the MCP server), not the database/server/API trio:
    draw what the story calls, not the generic data centre.

ADAPT IT: the MCP server can be any private endpoint the hub routes to (a spoke VNet,
a server behind a central firewall) — move it, keep the path. Another AI caller (an
agent, an App) replaces Genie One the same way. On AWS, PNG supports serverless DBR
only (Private Preview); do not draw Genie One through an AWS PNG unless the user says
it is supported for them.

items.title: Lakeflow Connect on-prem agent with front-end Private Link
items.prompt:
LAKEFLOW CONNECT FROM ON-PREMISES WITH NO INBOUND CONNECTION: THE ON-PREM AGENT
(AZURE, FRONT-END PRIVATE LINK)

architecture.md. Read reference/style-networking.md first.

HOW IT WORKS ON DATABRICKS (use this to adapt the diagram to the user's setup):
  • For customers whose security policy blocks ANY connection from the cloud into the
    on-premises network, but allows outbound HTTPS 443. The agent pushes data out, so
    there is no PNG, no reverse SSH tunnel and no open inbound firewall port. It is a
    Databricks-native replacement for the ADF Self-Hosted Integration Runtime (SHIR).
  • The agent runs next to the source databases, on the customer's own Linux x86_64
    host (it needs a PostgreSQL 14+ database for its repository, the Databricks ODBC
    driver and the source drivers: Oracle Instant Client, msodbcsql18). It reads the
    data locally and only ever connects OUT over HTTPS 443; Databricks never connects
    in to the agent.
  • Over ExpressRoute or VPN, the agent (1) signs in and sends SQL statements through
    the workspace endpoint, via the front-end Private Link endpoint in the hub; and
    (2) uploads Parquet files to a Unity Catalog managed volume through the storage
    private endpoint.
  • A Lakeflow Connect serverless pipeline then reads the staged files through the
    NCC private endpoint rule to the storage, and writes them to Delta tables in
    Unity Catalog.
  • Limits (Private Preview): full refresh only, no CDC in this release; SQL Server
    and Oracle only. Jobs are configured and scheduled in the agent's local UI; they
    cannot be triggered from the workspace.

WHAT IT DEMONSTRATES (layout):
  • The top level runs in the direction connections are OPENED: on-premises → agent →
    ExpressRoute / VPN → hub gateway → private endpoints → Unity Catalog storage and the
    workspace. The traffic starts on-premises, so on-premises is on the left.
  • Three paths, three line styles: the agent's upload (red, solid), its sign-in and
    SQL statements (red, dashed), and the serverless pipeline reading the staged files
    (dark, solid). The shared stretch (agent → gateway) is drawn once.
  • The pipeline's edge runs right → left on purpose: it is the one connection that
    starts in Databricks, and it ends at the customer's storage, not on-premises.
  • The workspace VNet is one card under the hub, joined by a dashed peering line.

ADAPT IT: with CDC needed (and inbound allowed through a PNG), use
lakeflow-cdc-png-azure.jsonc instead. With no ExpressRoute / VPN, the agent reaches
the public workspace and storage endpoints over the internet on 443: drop the hub
and the private endpoints, keep the agent and its two outbound paths.

items.title: ML platform on Databricks
items.prompt:
ML PLATFORM — end-to-end machine learning on Databricks, composed as nested containers.

Four strands of the story, each one a row of the platform's middle column:
  strand 1  sources → medallion (+ Feature Store fork) → training → registry
  strand 2  batch scoring job ← registry; predictions land back in the medallion
  strand 3  real-time serving → app; app state in Lakebase (synced gold)
  strand 4  documents → vector search → RAG endpoint → app ·· AI Gateway
STRUCTURE (reference/layout.md). The top level is a row: the sources column, then the platform box.
  • The sources column (`equal: "w"`) holds the PDF docs (`track: "docs"`), Postgres and the sensors.
  • The platform box is a column: a banner row (the db-platform wordmark and the governance
    bar, spread by `justify: "between"`), then a body row of three columns:
      – data: the medallion, alone in its column (it is tall, so nothing sits under it)
      – ml: three rows, the RAG path (vector search → RAG endpoint), the training path
        (training → registry) and the scoring path (batch scoring, real-time serving)
      – apps: the AI Gateway, the app and Lakebase
  • Shared tracks line the strands up across the columns: `docs` (PDFs and vector search),
    `train` (medallion and training), `serve` (real-time serving and the app).

What it demonstrates:
  • medallion-table `params.feature_store` → a Feature Store fork + `@out-fs`
    (training reads FEATURES, not raw gold); `@out-gold` feeds Lakebase.
  • the medallion is TALL and has its column to itself, so its height needs no clearance.
  • `lakeflow-jobs` relabeled as a batch scoring job (there is no dedicated
    type) — one tile, one label, no hidden description.
  • the RAG branch on its own row, and the AI Gateway next to the app whose
    model calls it governs (a short edge, not a long line across the diagram).
  • the platform box wraps the Databricks part only; the wordmark and the governance bar
    share its banner row.
This is a detail view. For a one-slide overview keep one serving story
(training → registry → real-time app) and move batch/RAG to a second tab.

items.title: Model promotion across platforms
items.prompt:
REFERENCE — a MULTI-PHASE RELAY: one artifact handed across trust boundaries
(here: author → hand off through an external platform → execute + decide on
Databricks → verify + serve back on the external platform). Read this when the
ask is a PIPELINE OF PHASES, not a single-platform flow: "promote models through
our existing ML platform with Databricks in the middle", "migration phases",
"dev → staging → prod with a gate between".

WHAT IT TEACHES (the pattern, distilled from a real customer diagram that went
through five review rounds):

  1. CHEVRON PHASE BANNERS name the sequence. One `type:"shape", shape:"chevron"`
     per phase, numbered, carrying the platform attribution ("· Databricks"). Each
     banner is the first child of its phase box and carries the same `track`, so the four
     banners sit on one line. The chevron IS the phase label — the phase boxes are
     left UNTITLED so the two never duplicate. A reader follows the banner 1→2→3→4; the
     edges only show data flow.
  2. LEVEL TOPS. The four phase boxes are the columns of one top-level row, and each
     phase starts with its banner. Keep the banners on the same track, so every banner and
     box top sits on one line. A phase with a different first child breaks the row.
  3. HAND-OFFS STAY SHORT: the receiving tile shares a `track` with the sender, or the
     next one. Inside a phase, steps stack vertically — that is the idiom, not a mistake;
     the banner carries the sequence, so the within-column chains don't need to be horizontal.
  4. THE DATA PLANE READS AS ITS OWN MINI-FLOW. Inside the Databricks phase the
     top row is one horizontal line: orchestrator → feature pipeline → training.
     The governance chain (registry → gate) drops below training, where the
     story says the decision happens.
  5. ARROWS. Static exports draw an arrowhead on every `flow:true` edge
     automatically; the explicit `arrow:"end"` here also gives the NON-flow
     hand-off edges a direction on the live canvas.
  6. PLAIN LANGUAGE ON TILES. "Classic ML training", "evaluation gate",
     "feature pipeline" — the demo's internal job/schema/SP names live in the
     LEGEND, not on the tiles. Subtitle budget: ~20–25 chars on a 220px source.
  7. A TILE MUST EARN ITS PLACE. There is no "raw data" satellite feeding the
     medallion from outside the frame: the medallion's bronze layer IS the
     landing point. (And if an asset's placement is itself the claim — "this
     data never transits the control plane" — the absence of an edge carries
     it; say so in `ai_reasoning`.)

PITFALLS:
  • A banner is the first child of its phase box, a chevron `shape` with the phase's
    `track`. Do not place it with `at`: a hand-placed banner drifts when the box moves.
  • Chevron text must clear the point + notch (≈ 2×34px of inset): ~28 chars
    max on a 336px banner at fontSize 18. Abbreviate platforms the audience
    knows ("AML", "AWS") when it's tight.
  • A tall composite (medallion-table renders ~126px) is taller than the other tiles
    beside it. `align: "start"` keeps the row's tops on one line.
  • ONE level of nesting is usually enough: a "Unity Catalog" box nested in
    the Databricks phase box reads as noise. The UC registry + gate TILES
    carry the governance presence.

PNG NETWORK TOPOLOGY: THE PNG SUBNET IN THE HUB OF A HUB-AND-SPOKE NETWORK (AZURE)

architecture.md. Read reference/style-networking.md first.

HOW IT WORKS ON DATABRICKS (use this to adapt the diagram to the user's network):
  • A Private Network Gateway (PNG) injects a Databricks-managed NIC into a dedicated
    /28 subnet of ONE customer network. Serverless traffic leaves through that NIC as
    if it originated there, so it can reach resources in that network and in networks
    transitively connected to it.
  • In a hub-and-spoke network the hub holds the shared services: the firewall, the
    bastion and the virtual gateway (VPN / ExpressRoute) to on-premises. Putting the
    PNG subnet IN THE HUB gives serverless one entry point that is already connected to
    on-premises (through the hub's gateway) and to the spokes (through peering).
  • The customer owns the path: DNS, routes and firewall rules must let serverless
    traffic from the PNG subnet reach each target. Nothing is configured on the
    gateway or the peerings for Databricks.
  • Limits to plan for: 10 NCCs per region per account, 2 PNGs per NCC. A common
    split is one NCC per environment and/or business unit.

WHAT IT DEMONSTRATES (layout):
  • A pure topology, no traffic arrows: networks as `box`es containing their subnets,
    each subnet a `box` around one icon. The top level is a row: on-premises → the link →
    the hub → the spokes. Inside the hub, a column of the firewall and gateway subnets sits
    beside a column of the bastion and PNG subnets.
  • The PNG subnet is the only Databricks element: an orange border (`style.border`)
    picks it out from the customer's subnets instead of a second colour scheme.
  • Peerings are grey dashed two-way lines. The VPN / ExpressRoute link is a logo between the
    two gateway subnets; the on-prem gateway, the link and the hub gateway share `track: "t2"`,
    so that line is straight.

a spoke of its own, or a spoke that must stay isolated: see
png-topology-isolated-spoke.jsonc. The traffic path through the PNG itself: see
serverless-png-azure.jsonc. On AWS the hub is a VPC behind a Transit Gateway.

architecture.md. Read reference/style-networking.md first.

architecture.md. Read reference/style-networking.md first.

HOW IT WORKS ON DATABRICKS (use this to adapt the diagram to the user's network):
  • An alternative when a Private Network Gateway (PNG) is not an option. Serverless
    reaches the customer network through a PRIVATE ENDPOINT RULE in the workspace's
    Network Connectivity Configuration (NCC), here pointing at an Azure Application
    Gateway v2 instead of a Private Link Service.
  • The customer creates two subnets in the hub VNet: one for the Application Gateway
    and one for its Private Link Configuration (the private IP addresses the private
    endpoint connects to). The gateway needs a standard public IP and frontend IP type

items.prompt:
SERVERLESS → ON-PREMISES ON AZURE WITHOUT PNG: PRIVATE LINK SERVICE + LOAD BALANCER + PROXY VMs

architecture.md. Read reference/style-networking.md first.

HOW IT WORKS ON DATABRICKS (use this to adapt the diagram to the user's network):
  • The fallback when a Private Network Gateway (PNG) is not an option (e.g. the
    customer does not accept Public Previews). Serverless compute runs in the
    Databricks-managed plane; it reaches the customer network through a PRIVATE
    ENDPOINT RULE in the workspace's Network Connectivity Configuration (NCC).
  • The customer creates an Azure Load Balancer as the frontend for their resources,
    and links it to an Azure Private Link Service (PLS). The NCC private endpoint rule
    targets that PLS, so Databricks gets a private endpoint into the customer's hub.
  • The load balancer's backend pool is a set of proxy VMs the customer runs
    (HAProxy, Squid, iptables, …) with custom routing to resources in the VNet and,
    through the hub's ExpressRoute / S2S VPN gateway, to on-premises.

    resources in the VNet and transitively connected networks (databases on VMs,
    custom TCP apps), and to on-premises over ExpressRoute or S2S VPN.
  • Watch out: not managed. The customer provisions, monitors and maintains the load
    balancer and the proxies (cost, overhead, deep proxy / routing knowledge); new
    targets usually mean a request to the infra team. Check first whether the target
    supports Private Link itself.
  • Pick it over App Gateway (reference/serverless-appgw-azure.jsonc) for ultra-low
    latency / high throughput, or when the customer already runs forwarding proxy VMs.
    If on-prem forbids inbound connections from the cloud, use the reverse SSH tunnel
    instead (reference/serverless-tunnel-azure.jsonc).

WHAT IT DEMONSTRATES (layout):
  • One hop per step, in traffic order, on one row: serverless → private endpoint rule →
    PLS → load balancer → proxy VMs → gateway → link → on-premises. The hops carry `track: "t1"`,
    and each subnet box wraps one hop, so the red path is a straight line.
  • The Databricks-owned hop (the NCC rule) sits in the Databricks box; everything
    the customer must run sits in the hub VNet.
  • The workspace VNet carries no serverless traffic: one card under the hub, joined by
    a dashed grey peering line.

VMs needed); GCP uses Private Service Connect with a service attachment. Drop the
proxy box if the target lives in the VNet and the load balancer can reach it directly.

items.title: Private Network Gateway on AWS
items.prompt:
SERVERLESS → PRIVATE / ON-PREMISES NETWORK ON AWS: PRIVATE NETWORK GATEWAY (PNG)

architecture.md. Read reference/style-networking.md first. The Azure version of the
same pattern is serverless-png-azure.jsonc.

HOW IT WORKS ON DATABRICKS (use this to adapt the diagram to the user's network):
  • Serverless compute runs in the Databricks-managed serverless compute plane, NOT
    in the customer's VPC. By default it cannot reach a private database, an on-prem
    server or an API behind the corporate firewall.
  • A Network Connectivity Configuration (NCC) is an account-level, per-region object
    that holds serverless private connectivity (private endpoint rules, and the PNG),
    attached to one or more workspaces. Limits: 10 NCCs per region per account, 2 PNGs
    per NCC.
  • A Private Network Gateway (PNG) is created INSIDE the NCC. Databricks places a
    managed network interface in a dedicated /28 subnet of the customer's VPC; serverless
    traffic leaves through it as if it originated in that VPC, so it follows the
    customer's own routes, DNS and firewalls (which the customer configures for the
    targets). On AWS the customer creates an IAM role in their account that Databricks
    uses to create and manage the PNG in that VPC.
  • Put the PNG subnet in the VPC that already routes to on-prem (here a shared services
    VPC attached to a Transit Gateway): traffic then rides the existing Transit Gateway
    and Direct Connect / Site-to-Site VPN to the data centre, and to anything
    transitively connected. One gateway replaces an endpoint per target resource.
  • The workspace VPC (private/public subnets for classic compute, an endpoint subnet) is
    attached to the same Transit Gateway. It is not on the serverless path; draw it only
    because the customer has it.
  • PNG does NOT carry traffic to services reached through interface / gateway endpoints
    (S3): those stay on NCC private endpoint rules.
  • AWS specifics: Enterprise tier; Private Preview; exactly ONE subnet (one AZ); serverless
    DBR workloads only. Provisioned through the API only (no Terraform yet).

WHAT IT DEMONSTRATES (layout):
  • The top level runs in traffic order: Databricks serverless plane → shared services VPC
    (PNG subnet) → Transit Gateway → Direct Connect gateway → the link → corporate data
    centre. The hops carry `track: "t1"`, so the red line is straight.
  • The IAM role is a control-plane relationship, not traffic: a grey dashed line under
    the path, its meaning in the role's `desc`, so it never competes with the red path.
  • A VPC with no serverless traffic (the workspace VPC) is ONE card listing its subnets;
    the Transit Gateway attachment is dashed grey.

ADAPT IT: keep only the networks the user names. With Site-to-Site VPN only, the VPN
attaches to the Transit Gateway and there is no Direct Connect gateway: drop that node.
With no Transit Gateway, the PNG subnet goes in whichever VPC has the route to the
targets. S3 or other AWS services: an NCC private endpoint, not the PNG.

items.title: Private Network Gateway on Azure
items.prompt:
SERVERLESS → PRIVATE / ON-PREMISES NETWORK ON AZURE: PRIVATE NETWORK GATEWAY (PNG)

architecture.md. Read reference/style-networking.md first.

HOW IT WORKS ON DATABRICKS (use this to adapt the diagram to the user's network):
  • Serverless compute runs in the Databricks-managed serverless compute plane, NOT
    in the customer's VNet. By default it cannot reach a private database, an
    on-prem server or an API behind the corporate firewall.
  • A Network Connectivity Configuration (NCC) is an account-level, per-region object
    that holds serverless private connectivity (private endpoint rules, and the
    PNG). It is attached to one or more workspaces. Limits: 10 NCCs per region per
    account, 2 PNGs per NCC; the usual split is one NCC per environment and/or BU.
  • A Private Network Gateway (PNG) is created INSIDE the NCC. Databricks injects
    a managed NIC into a dedicated /28 subnet of the customer's VNet, delegated to
    `Microsoft.Databricks/workspaces`. Serverless traffic leaves through that NIC as
    if it originated in the customer network, so it follows the customer's own
    DNS, routes and firewalls (which the customer must configure for the targets).
  • Put the PNG subnet in the HUB VNet when on-prem is reached through the hub: the
    traffic then rides the hub's VPN / ExpressRoute gateway to on-premises, and to
    anything transitively connected (spokes, a central firewall, a NAT or proxy to
    SaaS). One gateway replaces a private endpoint per target resource.
  • The workspace VNet (VNet injection: private/public subnets for classic compute,
    an endpoint subnet for private endpoints) is peered to the hub. It is not on the
    serverless path; draw it only because the customer has it.
  • PNG does NOT carry traffic to services reachable through private / service
    endpoints (Azure Storage accounts): those stay on NCC private endpoint rules.
  • Prerequisites: Premium tier; ExpressRoute or S2S VPN to on-prem; a /28 delegated
    subnet; an NCC (new or existing) with the PNG attached to the workspaces.
    Provisioned through the API only (no Terraform yet). Workloads on Azure: serverless
    DBR (notebooks, jobs), Apps, AI/ML. PNG on Azure is in Public Preview.

WHAT IT DEMONSTRATES (layout):
  • The top level runs in traffic order: Databricks serverless plane → the customer's hub
    VNet (PNG subnet, then gateway subnet) → the link → on-premises. The hops carry
    `track: "t1"`, so the whole path is one straight line.
  • Containment is nesting: subscription ⊃ hub VNet ⊃ subnets ⊃ resource. CIDRs in the
    box `subtitle`. Databricks-managed things sit in their own box, outside the subscription.
  • The traffic path is one colour (`#FF5F46`) with arrows; the peering is a dashed
    two-way grey line, so the reader sees what the serverless traffic does NOT use.
  • A network with no traffic on this slide (the workspace VNet) is ONE card listing
    its subnets, not nested boxes.

ADAPT IT: keep only the networks the user names. AWS PNG (Private Preview, serverless
DBR only): the same shape with a VPC, one /28 subnet in exactly one AZ and an IAM role
Databricks uses to create and manage the PNG. A storage account or S3 bucket is reached
through an NCC private endpoint, not the PNG: draw that instead when it is the ask.

items.title: AWS PrivateLink to your Network Load Balancer
items.prompt:
SERVERLESS → VPC / ON-PREMISES ON AWS WITHOUT PNG: PRIVATELINK TO YOUR OWN NLB

architecture.md. Read reference/style-networking.md first. When the Private Network
Gateway is an option, prefer serverless-png-aws.jsonc; this is the fallback.

HOW IT WORKS ON DATABRICKS (use this to adapt the diagram to the user's network):
  • Serverless compute runs in the Databricks-managed serverless plane, outside the
    customer's VPC. A private endpoint rule in the workspace's Network Connectivity
    Configuration (NCC) gives it a private, dedicated connection to ONE endpoint
    service in the customer's account, over AWS PrivateLink.
  • The customer builds the far side: a Network Load Balancer (NLB) as the front for
    the resources, with one listener per dedicated port (e.g. 1521, 3306) routing to a
    target group; targets are IPs in the VPC or on-premises. A VPC endpoint service
    exposes that NLB to Databricks.

    Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN. The workspace VPC is attached to the same
    Transit Gateway and is not on the serverless path.

    connected, or on-prem, and has no PrivateLink support of its own.

    the NLB (cost, overhead, networking skills), and app teams go back to the infra team
    for every new target (a new listener + target group).

  • The top level runs in traffic order: serverless plane → shared services VPC (endpoint
    service, then the NLB) → Transit Gateway → Direct Connect gateway → the link → data centre.
    `track` lines the hops up across the containers: `t1` on the path's outer hops, `t2` on the
    endpoint service and the NLB.
  • The NLB is one tile; its listeners → target groups are its `desc`, not separate
    boxes, because they are configuration of one resource (a card beside it would pull
    the path off the icon line). The two NLB subnets (one per AZ) are one box whose
    subtitle carries both CIDRs.
  • PrivateLink is carried by the endpoint service's `desc`, not an edge label: the
    edge crosses two box borders close together and a label has no clean slot there.

VPC: drop the Transit Gateway → on-prem chain and point the NLB at it. With Site-to-Site
VPN only, there is no Direct Connect gateway: drop that node. Azure: Private Link service
+ load balancer + proxy VMs (serverless-pls-azure.jsonc).

items.title: Private Service Connect on GCP
items.prompt:
SERVERLESS → ON-PREMISES ON GCP: PRIVATE SERVICE CONNECT + HYBRID NEG

architecture.md. Read reference/style-networking.md first.

HOW IT WORKS ON DATABRICKS (use this to adapt the diagram to the user's network):
  • Serverless compute runs in the Databricks-managed serverless plane, outside the
    customer's VPC. On GCP there is no Private Network Gateway: the private path to
    the customer network is a PSC endpoint, created as a PRIVATE ENDPOINT RULE in the
    workspace's Network Connectivity Configuration (NCC).
  • The customer publishes the target through a chain built in a hub VPC:
      1. a Hybrid Connectivity NEG (network endpoint group) whose endpoints are the
         target's private IP and port (an on-prem database, server or API);
      2. an internal TCP Proxy Load Balancer with the hybrid NEG as its backend. Its
         Envoy proxies run in a regional PROXY-ONLY subnet, and that subnet is
         advertised to on-prem over BGP (Cloud Router) so return traffic comes back;
      3. a PSC SERVICE ATTACHMENT fronting the load balancer's forwarding rule, using
         a dedicated PSC NAT subnet;
      4. the NCC private endpoint rule points at that service attachment.
  • The hub reaches on-prem over Cloud Interconnect or HA VPN (S2S); Cloud Router
    exchanges the routes. The workspace VPC is peered to the hub but is not on the
    serverless path.
  • This is the "Private Link service" pattern: use it when PNG is not an option. It
    is not managed: the customer provisions, monitors and maintains the load balancer
    and its configuration, one target (IP:port) per NEG endpoint.

WHAT IT DEMONSTRATES (layout):
  • The hops run in traffic order inside one hub row: the PSC NAT subnet → load balancer
    subnet → proxy-only subnet → hybrid NEG, then the link and on-premises. Each hop is a
    subnet box or a tile on `track: "t1"`, so the red path is one straight line.
  • What does not carry the data (Cloud Router's BGP, the peering) is grey and dashed.
  • A VPC with no traffic on this slide (the workspace VPC) is ONE card.

ADAPT IT: same chain on AWS (NLB + VPC endpoint service) and on Azure (Load
Balancer + Private Link service + proxy VMs): swap the subnets and icons. Several
targets: one NEG endpoint per target IP:port, not one diagram path each.

STYLE: NETWORKING — classic compute in a customer-managed VPC with PrivateLink.
Read reference/style-networking.md first.

HOW IT WORKS ON DATABRICKS (AWS): the control plane runs in a Databricks-managed
account. Classic compute runs in the customer's own VPC (customer-managed VPC),
one private subnet per availability zone, no public IPs. PrivateLink has two
independent halves:
  • back-end: the clusters reach the control plane through two interface VPC
    endpoints in the workspace VPC, one for the workspace REST API and one for
    the secure cluster connectivity (SCC) relay. Put them in their own small
    endpoint subnet.
  • front-end: users reach the web app and REST API through an interface
    endpoint in a transit VPC that their network (VPN / Direct Connect) reaches.
    It is a different endpoint from the back-end ones.
The root bucket is S3 in the customer account, reached through an S3 gateway
endpoint, so it sits outside the VPC. On Azure the same picture is VNet
injection + front-end / back-end Private Link; on GCP, Private Service Connect.

HOW IT IS BUILT (reference/layout.md):
  • The top level is a row in traffic order: users | customer account |
    Databricks control plane. Every PrivateLink edge then runs left → right.
  • Inside the workspace VPC, a row: the AZ subnets (a column group), then the
    endpoint subnet, closest to the control plane. Compute → endpoint →
    control plane is one direction, with no line crossing a subnet.
  • Tracks line each endpoint up with what it reaches: `fe` (users, front-end
    endpoint, web app), `scc` (SCC endpoint, relay).
  • Boundary facts (CIDR, "Databricks-managed") live in the box `subtitle`.

This is JSONC for YOU to read. When you write `architecture.md`, emit PLAIN

What it demonstrates:
  • Five columns, in reading order: sources → ingest → medallion → serve → consume.
    The ingest and medallion columns sit side by side in one Lakeflow box. The serve
    column sits beside it inside one platform box, with the db-platform wordmark as its
    first child. External consumers stay outside the platform box.
  • Existing extraction is REUSED (a tinted multi-source group) rather than
    rebuilt; each source has the one ingestion path that fits it.
  • A vertical medallion (Bronze → Silver → Gold, `@b` → `@t`).
  • External BI connects through Databricks SQL. The SQL tile is taller and sits in the
    middle of the serve column, so its three branches leave at different heights.
  • The platform box and the source tiles are placed with `at` (the exception in
    reference/layout.md), so they can be set by hand. Use nesting for any new diagram.
